description: We’re building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer — a fun, browser-based game that teaches kids real astronaut skills through hands-on missions. Think playful space adventures backed by actual NASA concepts. Our goal: make a polished, award-worthy entry. We’re a passionate team strong in game dev, web, and AI, and we’re looking for teammates who love coding, game design, art/animation, and storytelling. Come help us send kids to space! 🚀
summary:
ASTRONUT: Base Blunder is a browser game that lets kids aged 7–12 run an outpost on the Moon and Mars. Players survive three short missions: catching the low Sun at the Moon's south pole, riding out a Mars dust storm, and getting through an "SOS" when Earth sinks below the lunar horizon and all contact is lost.

Each in-game day has three steps. In the morning the player picks one problem to fix, and the problems they skip come back at night. At midday they drag system cards onto a 3D base; every card costs power, and oxygen, water and food are linked, so no choice is free. At night a real event plays out, such as a solar storm taken from NASA's DONKI space weather records.

The game turns real mission trade-offs into decisions a child can feel: shelter from radiation or run the lab, wait minutes for Earth's answer or decide alone. It runs in any browser with no download or account.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRONUT is a resource-management game with three missions of three sols (days) each, about 10 minutes in total.

- Morning: choose one of three problems or opportunities. Skipped problems cause damage that night, so players learn to prioritise.

- Midday: drag system cards onto the base (oxygen maker, water recycler, greenhouse, storm shelter, Earth dish, lab, gym, ice miner). Each card costs power. Cards that need water must be linked to a water source or they drain the tank. The 3D base updates live: buildings appear, status lights change colour, solar panels turn.

- Night: an event resolves and the player sees what changed and why, with a short fact and its source.

THE THREE MISSIONS

1. Moon South Pole: the Sun stays within about 1.5° of the horizon, so players aim their solar panels each morning. Better aim means more power.

2. Mars Dust Storm: sunlight drops day by day. Messages from Earth arrive after a real light delay of 3–22 minutes (shortened in play), so a storm warning can arrive too late.

3. SOS: Earth drops below the horizon for two sols. Players diagnose an oxygen leak from clues, repair it, and rely on their own lab sensors for storm warnings.

HOW IT TEACHES

Every decision has a cost. The storm shelter uses power that could run the lab. The Earth dish costs power but is the only source of warnings. The oxygen maker consumes water, and water recycling consumes power. A "NUT Meter" shows crew health, mood, sleep and radiation dose, the same things flight surgeons track. Failure is not punishing: a failed mission explains what went wrong and offers a retry.

Two difficulty levels match the age range. Junior (7–9) tracks only oxygen, power and radiation. Cadet (10–12+) adds water and food. Events are reshuffled every game for replay value. Scientific terms such as sol, kWh and mSv are explained in plain language when tapped.

USE OF NASA DATA

- Solar storms are drawn from four real events recorded in NASA's DONKI database (2017-09-10, 2021-10-28, 2024-05-11, 2024-06-08). They are archived records embedded in the game, not a live feed, and are labelled that way.

- Lunar lighting conditions come from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter findings.

- Life-support figures use NASA values: about 0.84 kg of oxygen per person per day and 98% water recovery on the ISS.

- Three real NASA images appear in the game with credits: the Sun during the September 2017 X8.2 flare (SDO), a Martian sunset (Curiosity), and Shackleton Crater (Scientific Visualization Studio, from LRO data).

Real images are tagged as real; generated artwork is tagged as illustration.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D base and the Web Audio API for sound. It includes a web app manifest and service worker for offline play. No server, account or installation is needed.

CREATIVITY

The base is both the game board and the lesson: what a player builds is what they see in 3D. The communication delay is something players wait through, not just read about. Each night the base's numbers can be played back as a short melody, so children can hear whether their base is healthy.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Reading level for ages 7–12, a small number of resources for younger players, phone and desktop layouts, playing without sound, and keeping every number traceable to a source listed in the in-game Field Manual.
